gap: No result ChatGPT got states how much current these AC/DC TIG machines draw from the wall on 110/120 V. YesWelder rates the TIG-200P ACDC PRO at 50 A input on 110 V for its 140 A maximum, which is more than three times the 15 A rating of an ordinary NEMA 5-15 household outlet. On 120 V, PrimeWeld TIG225X owners are told by Jody Collier (Weldmonger) to expect aluminum only up to about 0.100 in.
standout_why: Compared against homewelder.com (cited), woodworking-projects.com/hobby-tig-welder (cited) and welderverdict.com (top result). homewelder already explains AC oxide cleaning ('electrode-positive half of the AC cycle does the cleaning') and says machines cap out at 120–150 A on 110/120 V. woodworking-projects says '~120A on 120V … limiting for aluminum' and '1/8″ wants 130–160A'. welderverdict covers HF vs lift start for aluminum. None of them gives the input-current side: what the machine pulls from the outlet next to what a household 15/20 A receptacle is rated for. None gives a named aluminum thickness limit on 120 V for a specific candidate either. So the basic mechanism (AC for aluminum, lower output on 120 V) is already covered, but the outlet-current mismatch is new.
decides: It answers ChatGPT's own follow-up question, 'Regular 120V household outlet only'. On a household outlet, every candidate is power-limited for aluminum, and the reason is the outlet's current rating, not the welder's price class. So the pick depends on the outlet more than the brand. If the shopper has or can add a 240 V circuit, any of the 200 A AC/DC machines works for steel and aluminum. If they have only a 120 V outlet, the cheapest AC/DC unit with a pedal included (LOTOS TIG200ACDC, $399.98) is the sensible buy, because extra money for 200–225 A buys nothing they can use. The page should tell 120 V-only shoppers to plan on 240 V before spending more.
